usage_notes.narrative: For maj7 as tonic resolution, Vaartstra prescribes isolating and playing the guide tones (3rd and 7th) in half or quarter notes through the entire song form before attempting melodic improvisation. 'It's a great practice to play them isolated with either half notes or quarter notes through the entire form of a song.' Chapter 2, p. 38.

When navigating I-i minor shifts (e.g., Cmaj7 to Cmin7), Vaartstra prescribes adjusting only the b3 and b7 -- the defining quality intervals -- while keeping all other notes constant. 'The only difference between a major 7 chord and a minor 7 chord is the minor has a b3 and a b7. Make this adjustment and you are good to go!' Chapter 8, p. 122.

Vaartstra explicitly licenses targeting upper extensions (9th, 11th, 13th) over any maj7 chord in improvisation. 'Most chords in jazz are labeled as 7 chords. But this doesn't mean you can't add or target extensions and alterations of these chords. Utilizing the 9th, 11th and 13th can have a powerful effect.' Chapter 8, p. 132.

Vaartstra prescribes recognizing maj7 chords as targets of the backdoor dominant device: the bVII7 approaches the I maj7 by whole step rather than the conventional V7. 'A backdoor dominant is a dominant 7th chord that substitutes the V7 chord for a bVII7 chord approaching the I chord by a whole step. Example: Bb7-Cmaj7.' Chapter 11, p. 177.

For dominant 7 chords in ii-V-I progressions, Vaartstra prescribes voice-leading the 7th of the dom7 to the 3rd of the next chord by stepwise motion. 'Notice how the 7th of each chord resolves to the 3rd of the next chord... the closest step-wise motion you can make from the 7th of a chord in this ii-V-I, is the 3rd of the next. That's voice leading.' Chapter 2, p. 37.

Vaartstra prescribes treating any dom7 that precedes a non-tonic diatonic chord as a secondary dominant (tonicization), and expanding it with a ii chord in front to form a ii-V. 'It's just as easy to add a ii chord in front of it to create a ii-V chord progression. Where there is a V chord, you can almost always add a ii in front of it.' Chapter 5, p. 78; Chapter 10, p. 158.

Vaartstra prescribes freely converting diatonic minor chords to dominant 7ths as a core jazz harmonic practice. 'It is entirely normal and acceptable to turn minor chords in the diatonic series into dominant 7th chords.' This is applied in the analysis of Sweet Georgia Brown's VI7 opener and recurs across multiple standards. Chapter 6, p. 95; also Chapter 2, p. 33.

For improvising over dom7 chords, Vaartstra prescribes the Mixolydian scale as the primary pitch collection: 'The easiest way to think of a Mixolydian scale is a major scale with a b7. Formula: 1-2-3-4-5-6-b7.' Students are told to use it as a pitch collection -- not a linear drill -- and to practice chord-tone patterns starting on different chord tones each bar. Chapter 6, p. 98-99.

Vaartstra prescribes recognizing that any dominant 7 chord may be replaced by the dominant 7 chord whose root lies a tritone away. 'Sometimes this is called a tritone substitution, meaning, a chord is being substituted by another chord with a root a tritone interval away.' He also offers the alternative reading of interpreting the substituting chord as a chromatic passing chord between ii and I. Chapter 8, p. 122.

Vaartstra prescribes the backdoor dominant as a V7 substitute: the bVII7 approaches the tonic by whole step and may be preceded by its own ii chord to form a full backdoor ii-V. 'The Bbmin7-Eb7 is really acting as a backdoor ii-V into the Fmaj7.' Players should also learn the dual interpretation -- the same dom7 chord can be read simultaneously as V7/IV or as a backdoor dominant into I. Chapter 11, p. 177-178.

For min7 in its ii-chord function, Vaartstra prescribes entering the arpeggio on whichever chord tone is nearest to the last note played in the prior chord, not necessarily the root: 'Whatever the last note played in a particular bar was, I move to the nearest chord tone of the next chord.' Regardless of starting tone, arpeggios always proceed in order (Root-3-5-7 or any rotation). Chapter 4, p. 65.

Vaartstra prescribes treating a song-opening vi min7 as the initiator of a diatonic cycle of 4ths rather than as an isolated tonic substitute. 'Notice that it starts with the vi chord. This vi chord starts a long cycle of 4ths all the way through the Dbmaj7 in bar 5. Everything here is diatonically pure to the key center.' Chapter 10, p. 158.

For min7 chords functioning as modal tonics (e.g., D Dorian in So What), Vaartstra prescribes abandoning the guide-tone framework entirely and using the Dorian mode (formula: W-H-W-W-W-H-W; scale tones: 1-2-b3-4-5-6-b7) as the pitch collection. 'There is no need to identify the guide tones... the best way to improvise over modal harmony is by using modes.' Players should use sparse, space-conscious phrasing modeled on Miles Davis. Chapter 7, p. 103-108.

Vaartstra prescribes the minor iv chord (e.g., Abmin6 or Abmin7 functioning as iv in a major key) as a substitute for the plain V7 before the I chord, and further allows expanding it to a full backdoor ii-V (e.g., Abmin7-Db7) or compressing it to a single Db7. 'Musicians will play an Abmin6, which functions as the minor IV chord... You can also turn that Abmin6 into a ii-V (Abmin7-Db7), or you can even just play a Db7.' Chapter 5, p. 80.

Vaartstra proscribes using major 3rds or major 7ths when improvising over the iv minor chord. 'Don't get too hung up on the iv minor chord. In your improvisation, you will simply want to consider the difference in the chord quality. Don't be playing major thirds or major 7ths!' Chapter 4, p. 63.

Vaartstra prescribes distinguishing a closing cycle-of-4ths built from minor ii-Vs from the more common dominant ii-V cycle. 'This cycle of 4ths is different than we have seen before in that they are a series of minor ii-V's.' Scale and note choices must reflect the minor quality. Chapter 11, p. 179.

Vaartstra prescribes treating min7b5 (half-diminished) as the ii chord in minor-key ii-V-i progressions, formula Root-b3-b5-b7, and identifies it as such within the hybrid ii-V-I construction: 'A hybrid ii-V-I is when a minor ii-V-i is mixed with a major ii-V-I. The ii and V are borrowed from the minor key... Example: Dmin7(b5)-G7(b9)-Cmaj7.' Chapter 11, p. 179. For improvisation, target chord tones directly derived from the formula. Chapter 4, p. 64.

Vaartstra prescribes a dual reading of min7b5 in context: the same chord may be analyzed as either a ii7b5 of the secondary key (standard minor ii-V reading) or as the iiib5 within the parent tonal center when the chord pair is reread as iii(b5)-VI7. 'The Gmin7(b5) can also be thought of as the iiib5 (adding a b5 to the iii minor) and a VI7... if we combine this understanding with the ii-V of ii concept everything ties together.' Chapter 5, p. 79.

Vaartstra prescribes interpreting min7b5 in context of its resolution target rather than in isolation: 'If we look at a Gmin7(b5) and a C7(b9) as separate chords, they are confusing. But if we look at them as resolving to an Fmin7, then we have something functional to understand.' Improvisation should reflect that relational function. Chapter 5, p. 79.

Vaartstra prescribes using dom7b9 (e.g., G7b9) as the V chord in the hybrid ii-V-I, borrowed from the parallel minor key while still resolving to the major I: 'A hybrid ii-V-I is when a minor ii-V-i is mixed with a major ii-V-I. The ii and V are borrowed from the minor key, but they resolve to the major I. Example: Dmin7(b5)-G7(b9)-Cmaj7.' Chapter 11, p. 179.

Vaartstra prescribes treating a dom7b9 chord as analytically equivalent to a diminished 7 on its 3rd: 'F#dim7: F#-A-C-Eb / D7(b9): D-F#-A-C-Eb... You can think of the F#dim7 as a rootless D7(b9).' For improvisation, either chord tones of the dim7 or the full dom7b9 pitch set will serve. Chapter 9, p. 141.

Vaartstra prescribes understanding a passing dim7 in two simultaneous ways: as a rootless dominant b9 substitute for the chord a major 2nd below, and as a chromatic passing chord connecting adjacent diatonic chords by bass half-step. 'On a compositional level the F#dim7 is functioning as more than just a substitution. It's also creating a chromatic passing note, in this case the bass note, to connect the I chord with the ii chord.' Chapter 9, p. 142.

For improvisation over passing dim7 chords, Vaartstra prescribes targeting the chord tones of the implied dominant b9 that the dim7 substitutes. 'Remember that it is being substituted for the VI7b9 chord, so any of those chord tones will serve you well.' The Whole-Half diminished scale (W-H-W-H-W-H-W-H) is taught as the theoretical note resource for this context. Chapter 9, p. 145.

Vaartstra prescribes reading a biii diminished 7 chord in a cycle-of-4ths context (e.g., All the Things You Are) as a purely chromatic connector rather than a dominant substitute: 'The biii diminished isn't necessarily replacing anything. Its primary job is to connect the iii chord to the ii chord chromatically.' Improvise through it as a brief chromatic link. Chapter 10, p. 161.

Vaartstra prescribes recognizing the i minor chord substitution on a major-key I chord (e.g., Cmin7 replacing Cmaj7 in bar 3 of On Green Dolphin Street) as a deliberate quality shift, not an error, and adjusting improvisation by altering only the b3 and b7. 'The form starts right on the tonic... until we get to bar 3 where we make a sudden switch to the i minor.' Adjust only the defining 3rd and 7th in melodic lines. Chapter 8, p. 122.

While Vaartstra does not label the So What chord explicitly as 'sus4', he prescribes using D Dorian (W-H-W-W-W-H-W) as the pitch collection over the modal chord structure of So What -- a stacked-4ths voicing implying suspended quality -- and models Miles Davis's approach: 'He generally plays within the Dorian mode, with exceptions of course and occasional chromatic approach notes.' For modal voicings implying sus/quartal quality, guide tones are explicitly not required. Chapter 7, p. 103-114.
